before: the evidence became clear to you
after: Clarity carries an ethical threshold: after truth becomes unmistakable, earlier bonds or requests cannot continue unchanged.
reason: The focus says تَّبَيَّنَ, and 9:113 repeats مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ before changing what believers may do. That is a real post-clarity echo, though the ruling about intercession and kinship does not describe ʿĀd's or Thamud's diversion.

before: their dwellings are evidence of what happened
after: The prior account leaves a people collapsed inside their homes, and this verse immediately presents ʿĀd and Thamud's dwellings as evidence. Habitation is the surviving witness of judgment: residents are gone, while the place remains legible.
reason: The preceding 29:37 says فَأَصْبَحُوا فِي دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ, and 29:38 follows with مِّن مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ. Their adjacency makes the home in the destruction account the kind of material trace that later audiences can inspect.

before: they were capable of insight
after: The focus's insight-capable people sit beside an audience asked whether it cannot see the punishment. Visual access becomes a test of recognition: an unmistakable consequence can still be dismissed by misnaming what is seen.
reason: The focus calls them مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ, while 52:15 asks أَمْ أَنتُمْ لَا تُبْصِرُونَ as people confront punishment. The question turns sight from mere access into recognition, matching the tension between visible evidence and a failure to follow it.

branch: inter-ayah: judgment of the named peoples
before: ʿĀd and Thamud appear among past peoples
after: The phrase كُلًّا أَخَذْنَا بِذَنۢبِهِۦ supplies the verdict immediately after the paired names: each earlier people was seized for its own offense. The following list of distinct punishments turns their dwellings into evidence of judged communities, not merely abandoned architecture.
reason: 29:40's فَكُلًّا أَخَذْنَا بِذَنۢبِهِۦ directly explains the preceding list that includes ʿĀd and Thamud. Its catalogue of different punishments makes the focus's visible dwellings part of a sequence of consequences assigned to past peoples.

before: the devil adorned their deeds
after: Verse 3:14 repeats زُيِّنَ with حب الشهوات as its object, where 29:38 says the devil adorned their deeds. The shifted object makes the focus's broad أعمال concretely audible as worldly desire: attraction can be worked over until wrongdoing presents itself as desirable.
reason: The passive زُيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ in 3:14 makes desires attractive, while the focus uses active وَزَيَّنَ for the devil's adornment of أعمالهم. The shared beautifying image lets desires sound like one material through which an act can be made appealing.

branch: inter-ayah: clarity followed by path choice
trigger_ar: مِنۢ بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ ٱلْهُدَىٰ وَيَتَّبِعْ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
before: they were turned away from the path
after: The sequence مِنۢ بَعْدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ followed by غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ fuses the focus's two poles, clarity and departure from a path. It makes the obstruction a choice after guidance is manifest, then names a final destination for that choice.
reason: 4:115 places تَبَيَّنَ الْهُدَى before وَيَتَّبِعْ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ, directly joining recognized guidance to following another way. The focus's عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ gains the same paradoxical setting: the way is available and clear, yet they are diverted from it.

before: they were described as perceptive

before: they were turned from the path

reason: The focus says فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, and 26:97 calls the speakers' state ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ. Clear error is a strong semantic counterpart to being turned from the way, but the verse offers no specific historical link to the named communities.

before: the former peoples were described as insightful

The pairing moves the evidence from ruins outside to signs within the observer, making sight a test of inward attention as well as physical viewing.
reason: The question أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ follows 51:20's signs in the earth and points to signs وَفِي أَنفُسِكُمْ. Set beside the focus's surviving مسَاكِن and مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ, it makes evidence both external and internal, while asking whether its observer truly perceives.

before: they were capable of insight
after: Verse 29:43 makes understanding examples a further step beyond their presentation. It echoes the focus's insight language, but its reference to parables does not directly identify the ruins as the example being understood.
reason: وَمَا يَعْقِلُهَآ إِلَّا ٱلْعَٰلِمُونَ distinguishes hearing or seeing an example from grasping it. That cognition can color مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ as a claim about discernment, though the focus's dwellings are not explicitly called a parable here.

branch: inter-ayah: desire as a route to misguidance
before: the devil turned them away through beautified deeds
after: The verbs يضلون and phrase بأهوائهم بغير علم describe people leading others astray through desires without knowledge. This supplies an appetite-driven channel for the focus's beautified أعمال and diversion from ٱلسَّبِيلِ, showing how attractive conduct can recruit others into misguidance.
reason: 6:119's لَيُضِلُّونَ بِأَهْوَائِهِم بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ names desire as an instrument of leading people astray. Alongside the focus's وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ, it makes the beautification-and-diversion sequence concrete as desire reshaping conduct.

trigger_ar: ءَايَٰتٍۭ بَيِّنَٰتٍۢ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَهْدِى مَن يُرِيدُ
before: the evidence became clear and people were diverted

reason: The wording ءَايَٰتٍۭ بَيِّنَٰتٍۢ and يَهْدِى in 22:16 places clear signs beside guidance. It activates both the focus's clarity verb تَّبَيَّنَ and its later path language, providing the positive response their history lacks.

before: they were diverted from the path

reason: The closing phrase فَقَدْ ضَلَّ سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ uses path language for a believer who takes the wrong allegiance described in the verse. It gives the focus's diversion a relational parallel, though it supplies little about the earlier peoples' particular cause.

trigger_ar: وَمَثَلًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ خَلَوْا۟ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ

reason: 24:34 pairs آيَاتٍ مُّبَيِّنَاتٍ with an example drawn from earlier peoples. That direct combination lets the focus's dwellings function as evidence and an admonitory example, not simply as a geographical remnant.

before: the people were described as perceptive
after: The idiom أَبْصِرْ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمِعْ attributes perfect seeing and hearing to God, forming a loose counterpoint to human مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ. The sight image is present, but it praises divine perception rather than explaining why the earlier peoples failed to act on insight.
reason: 18:26's أَبْصِرْ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمِعْ praises God's seeing and hearing beside the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ. The shared perception image is real, yet the divine subject makes this only a weak counterpoint to the humans who were diverted.

trigger_ar: مِنۢ بَعْدِ مَا عَقَلُوهُ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ
before: they were described as insight-capable
after: 2:75 describes a group who hear God's word, then distort it after understanding it, ending وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ. Those verbs map knowledge onto deliberate deformation of truth, sharpening the focus's paradox of insight-capable people whose actions are nonetheless turned away.
reason: The sequence مِنۢ بَعْدِ مَا عَقَلُوهُ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ makes understanding and knowledge precede distortion in 2:75. It activates the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ not as innocence, but as knowledge that can coexist with a wrongful course.

before: they were turned away from the path
after: The wording وَصَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ repeats the focus's obstruction verb and path target nearly exactly. By adding that the obstructors die in disbelief and are denied forgiveness, 47:34 extends diversion into a persistent moral course with an end.
reason: 47:34 directly pairs وَصَدُّوا with عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ, matching فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ in the focus. Its added condition of dying as disbelievers turns obstruction from an episode into a continuing stance with a stated consequence.

before: the evidence became manifest
after: The offer بِشَىْءٍ مُّبِينٍ echoes the focus's تَّبَيَّنَ through the field of manifest proof. It can color the dwellings as evidence to be examined, but Moses' challenge adds no link to the named peoples or their response.
reason: Moses' phrase بِشَىْءٍۢ مُّبِينٍۢ describes something clear or manifest, near the focus's claim that evidence تَّبَيَّنَ from the dwellings. This is a limited clarity echo without the focus's history of misdirection.

before: their dwellings are surviving evidence
after: 15:82 says the people carved houses from mountains while feeling secure, turning the focus's مسَاكِنِهِمْ into a built, apparently protected habitat. In the surrounding Hijr passage these stone-dwelling people receive signs and are struck, so the secure houses become part of the ruin testimony.
reason: The words يَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا ءَامِنِينَ supply a precise material image for the focus's dwellings. Their mountain-cut security sits beside the focus's ruined habitation, making the former shelter itself a trace of failed confidence.

before: the focus says evidence became clear from their dwellings
after: Addressing Hud, the speakers from ʿĀd say مَا جِئْتَنَا بِبَيِّنَةٍ, denying the clear evidence the focus later says their dwellings reveal. Their refusal to leave their gods despite that denial shows how a claim of absent proof can coexist with fixed commitment and diversion.
reason: In 11:53 Hud's interlocutors say مَا جِئْتَنَا بِبَيِّنَةٍ and refuse to abandon their gods; the surrounding passage identifies Hud's people as ʿĀd. That earlier denial of proof makes the focus's later تَّبَيَّنَ مِن مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ a pointed reversal: the remains now testify where they claimed no sign existed.

before: they were called insightful despite being diverted
after: The noun بَصَائِرُ beside هُدًى makes real perception and right direction a property of revelation, while the focus calls its people مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ yet says they were turned from the way. The contrast lets the rare participle sound like a faculty misused, measured against scripture's function as sight and guidance.
reason: 45:20 names the revelation بَصَائِرُ لِلنَّاسِ وَهُدًى, combining perception and guidance. Beside the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ and عَنِ السَّبِيلِ, it distinguishes insight that actually guides from the failed perception of people diverted from their way.

before: Thamud are named among peoples whose dwellings are evidence
after: 15:80 identifies the people of al-Hijr as deniers of messengers, while the neighboring passage recalls their given signs and mountain houses. This fills out the focus's Thamud reference with a concrete rejection, so the surviving dwelling evidence points back to a known refusal rather than ruin alone.
reason: The phrase كَذَّبَ أَصْحَٰبُ الْحِجْرِ الْمُرْسَلِينَ ties a named community to rejection of messengers. In its adjacent account of signs and mountain dwellings, it supplies the response behind the focus's Thamud-related remains.

before: they were described as perceptive
after: أَعْمَى أَبْصَٰرَهُمْ names blinded eyes, a sharp opposite to the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ. The contrast allows a later state of lost perception to sound against their insight, but the verse does not identify the same people or explain their diversion.
reason: 47:23 says God made some deaf and blinded their eyes, using أَبْصَارَهُمْ against the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ. The perceptual opposition is strong, but the verse supplies no specific link to ʿĀd, Thamud, or their visible dwellings.

before: the evidence became clear to the audience
after: يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ describes the white thread becoming distinguishable from the dark at dawn, repeating the focus's verb of becoming clear. This supplies a concrete image of clarity arriving through contrast, though the fasting boundary has no tie to the ruined communities.
reason: In 2:187 the light thread يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ from the dark thread; the verb matches the focus's تَّبَيَّنَ. Its concrete dawn distinction can echo evidence emerging into view, but nothing else in the fasting instruction connects to the focus.

branch: inter-ayah: signs until truth is clear
trigger_ar: ءَايَٰتِنَا فِى ٱلْءَافَاقِ وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ٱلْحَقُّ
before: the dwellings made evidence clear
after: The verse says signs in horizons and in themselves will be shown until it becomes clear they are truth, repeating the focus's pattern of evidence becoming manifest to an audience. reason: 41:53 pairs signs in the horizons and selves with حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ, echoing the focus's تَّبَيَّنَ لَكُم. The trigger broadens the focus's visible dwelling evidence into signs both outside and within observers, aimed at recognition of truth.

before: their dwellings are visible evidence
after: 2:259 begins with a person passing a village collapsed upon its roofs and asking how God will revive it after its death. It turns an abandoned settlement into a testable sign and repeats تَبَيَّنَ when the truth becomes clear, extending ruin evidence from past judgment to resurrection.
reason: The description قَرْيَةٍ وَهِىَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا gives another abandoned settlement as the setting for a question about divine power. When understanding later becomes clear, the focus's مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ can likewise be heard as material evidence with implications beyond architecture.

branch: inter-ayah: public obstruction of the path
before: the devil turned the people away from the path

reason: 9:34 uses وَيَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ, nearly the same verb-and-target phrase as the focus's فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ. Its setting among authorities who consume people's wealth shows one public form that blocking God's way can take.

before: the people had insight
after: وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ supplies a sharp knowledge marker beside مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ, describing people who knowingly lie about God. The parallel suggests deliberate rather than innocent error, though the trust dispute does not explain the focus's Satanic beautification.
reason: 3:75 closes its account of lying about God with وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ, a strong marker of awareness beside the focus's مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ. It supports a cautious parallel between knowing and acting wrongly, but has no direct path or Satan image.

branch: inter-ayah: travel and inspect past outcomes
trigger_ar: فَسِيرُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَٱنظُرُوا۟ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ
before: their dwellings make past judgment visible
after: The command فَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَانظُرُوا followed by the fate of deniers turns travel into an exercise in reading historical aftermath. It supplies a method for the focus's claim that fate is evident from the dwellings: inspect the remains and infer what happened to their former inhabitants.
reason: 3:137 commands the audience to travel and look at the end of deniers, the same kind of inference the focus invites from the dwellings. The phrase كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ makes visible remains a lesson about historical outcome.

before: Satan adorned their deeds and diverted them

reason: The words ٱتَّخَذُوا الشَّيَاطِينَ أَوْلِيَاء and يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ give both the satanic agent and mistaken sense of guidance. They activate the focus's devil, beautified deeds, and insight paradox as parts of a single misdirection pattern.

before: the focus points to the dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamud

reason: The clause تَنْحِتُونَ الْجِبَالَ بُيُوتًا specifies impressive mountain houses, while its wording also recalls succeeding ʿĀd. With the prior verse addressing Thamud, the passage gives the focus's paired peoples a shared history of settled power under warning.

before: Thamud's dwellings remain as evidence

reason: The phrase فَأَصْبَحُوا فِي دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ places the destroyed people inside their own home, echoing the focus's مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ. The nearby Thamud account identifies the inhabitants and turns the residence into the setting of their end.

branch: inter-ayah: seeing the right path but refusing it
trigger_ar: وَإِن يَرَوْا۟ سَبِيلَ ٱلرُّشْدِ لَا يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلًۭا
before: they were insight-capable yet diverted
after: 7:146 explicitly says that people may see every sign and still refuse the path of right, choosing the path of error instead. These paired sight and path verbs enact the focus's paradox with unusual precision: the people can be described as insightful while their choices go the opposite way.
reason: 7:146's وَإِن يَرَوْا سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ لَا يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلًا directly combines seeing with rejecting a path. The focus likewise pairs مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ with being turned from ٱلسَّبِيلِ, so the other verse specifies a choice made despite perception.

branch: inter-ayah: the cry in Thamud's dwellings

reason: 11:67 places those seized by the cry in دِيَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ, a close image of the focus's dwellings after destruction. The continuation in 11:68 names Thamud, confirming that this house-bound catastrophe belongs to the people the focus lists.

reason: 11:68 says it is as though they never flourished there, then identifies Thamud, while 29:38 says the audience can see clearly from their dwellings. This creates a weak contrast between absent inhabitants and the testimony their place still carries.

reason: The paired names وَعَادٍ وَثَمُودَ reappear in 14:9, where the surrounding words say their messengers came with clear proofs and the people rejected them. The focus's visible remains thus belong to a larger record of named communities refusing evidence.

reason: The words ءَاتَيْنَاهُمْ ءَايَاتِنَا فَكَانُوا عَنْهَا مُعْرِضِينَ state that signs were given and then rejected. In the adjoining account of the people of al-Hijr and their homes, this makes the focus's Thamud evidence part of a known pattern of turning away despite signs.

trigger_ar: فَهِىَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا وَبِئْرٍۢ مُّعَطَّلَةٍۢ وَقَصْرٍۢ مَّشِيدٍ
before: their dwellings reveal an aftermath
after: 22:45 stacks a hollowed town, an abandoned well and a high-built palace after saying it was destroyed while unjust. These abandoned structures make the focus's ruined dwellings part of a recognizable landscape of judgment, where monumental construction survives its unjust inhabitants.
reason: The images خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا, بِئْرٍ مُعَطَّلَةٍ, and قَصْرٍ مَّشِيدٍ give concrete forms to a settlement emptied after its people were destroyed. They activate the focus's مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ as public material evidence rather than a bare mention of place.

branch: inter-ayah: external sight and inner blindness
trigger_ar: فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَعْمَى ٱلْأَبْصَٰرُ وَلَٰكِن تَعْمَى ٱلْقُلُوبُ
before: the former peoples were capable of insight
after: The follow-up asks whether travelers will grow hearts to reason and ears to hear, then says the eyes do not go blind, but hearts do. It turns the focus's visible dwellings and مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ into a test of inward reception: external sight alone does not guarantee that evidence is understood.
reason: 22:46 contrasts ٱلْأَبْصَارُ with hearts that go blind after asking about travel, reasoning, and hearing. Beside the focus's visible dwellings and insight-capable people, it makes the failure one of inward comprehension rather than access to evidence.

branch: inter-ayah: seeing ruined evidence without inference
trigger_ar: أَفَلَمْ يَكُونُوا۟ يَرَوْنَهَا بَلْ كَانُوا۟ لَا يَرْجُونَ نُشُورًۭا
before: the people were said to be insightful
after: 25:40 describes people passing a town rained upon with evil and asks whether they do not see it, then says they do not expect resurrection. It closely mirrors the focus's question of visible ruins and failed insight: an observer may see the trace but fail to infer the future it warns about.
reason: 25:40 combines an encountered ruined town with أَفَلَمْ يَكُونُوا يَرَوْنَهَا and the denial of resurrection. Those actual words parallel the focus's dwellings as visible proof and its مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ paradox: seeing a ruin need not mean grasping its warning.

before: they were turned away from the path
after: The Fatiha's repeated request ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ is recited at every prayer beside this focus's account of people turned from ٱلسَّبِيلِ. It frames the ruined peoples as a warning against diversion and the believer's recurring prayer as a request for the direction they lost.
reason: The focus says فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ, and the Fatiha repeatedly asks ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ. The direct path-and-guidance pairing makes the daily recited request answer the focus's account of people obstructed from the way.

branch: adjacent ayah: homes as failed refuge
before: their dwellings remain as evidence
after: The next verse's spider adopts بَيْتًا, but its house is the weakest of dwellings, while the focus's مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ are remains from which past failure becomes clear. Their adjacency sets habitation against falsely secure refuge: a building can be an image of failed reliance as well as evidence after collapse.
reason: 29:41 moves from the focus's visible مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ to a spider taking بَيْتًا and then calls its house the weakest of houses. That immediate change of dwelling image invites the reader to compare the failed shelter of past peoples with the fragile refuge built on false allies.
